children.note: Start here: what we mean by 'law', what it is for, and the basic ways lawyers sort it.
Law is a set of rules that the state backs with courts, police and penalties. A church rule or a family rule may matter a lot, but the state will not enforce it in court.
Law keeps order, settles disputes peacefully, protects rights and property, and lets people plan (for example, a duka owner can trust that a supplier contract will be enforced).
Everyone, including the government, must obey the law, and power must be used only as the law allows. In Kenya the Constitution itself says no one may claim state power except as it allows.

manas.q: What does 'the rule of law' mean?

children.note: Criminal law: the state prosecutes a wrong against society and can punish (jail, fine). Civil law: one person sues another for a remedy such as money, e.g. a matatu passenger suing for injuries.

manas.q: What is the main difference between a civil case and a criminal case?

children.note: Public law governs the state and its relations with people (constitutional, administrative, criminal law). Private law governs dealings between people (contract, torts, property, family).
Substantive law says what your rights and duties are. Procedural law says how you enforce them in court: filing, deadlines, evidence and appeals.

children.topic: Common law family vs civil law family
children.note: Kenya follows the common law tradition from England, where judges' decisions are a key source of law. Civil law countries (France, Germany) rely mainly on written codes.
Where a Kenyan lawyer looks to find the rule. Think of a ladder: the Constitution at the top, then Acts, then rules made under Acts, then judge-made and customary law to fill gaps.
The supreme law. It binds every person and every state organ, nationally and in the counties, and its validity cannot be challenged in any court.

manas.q: What is the highest law in Kenya?

children.topic: Any law in conflict is void
children.note: If any law, customary law included, clashes with the Constitution, it is void to the extent of the clash. So a 'law' that breaks the Bill of Rights cannot stand.
Written laws passed by Parliament, such as the Penal Code, the Law of Contract Act and the Evidence Act. Law-making power comes from the people and Parliament holds it at national level.
County assemblies also pass laws for their counties. They must stay within the Constitution and the powers given to counties.
Detailed rules, regulations and by-laws made by a minister or body under power given by an Act. The Act must set out the purpose, limits and standards of that power.
Rules developed by judges over centuries, first in England. Kenya received English common law in colonial times; today Kenyan courts develop it in line with the Constitution.
Fairness rules from the old English Court of Chancery that soften harsh common law, e.g. injunctions and trusts. When equity and common law clash, equity usually prevails.
This Act tells courts the order in which to use the sources: Constitution, written law, then common law and equity, and African customary law where relevant. Reviewer: confirm section numbers.
Community customs (e.g. on marriage, land and inheritance) still apply in many disputes. They must give way where they clash with the Constitution or written law.
Courts must encourage reconciliation, mediation, arbitration and traditional methods, but never where these break the Bill of Rights, justice and morality, or the law.
Muslim law applies to personal status, marriage, divorce and inheritance, only where all parties are Muslim and agree to the Kadhi's court.
General rules of international law, and treaties Kenya has ratified, form part of Kenyan law. This is a big change from the old view that treaties needed a separate Act.

manas.q: How do ratified treaties become part of Kenyan law under the 2010 Constitution?

children.note: Who decides cases, and where appeals go. Superior courts sit at the top; subordinate courts hear most everyday cases.
Superior courts: Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court and the two courts of equal status. Subordinate courts: magistrates', Kadhis', courts martial and other courts or tribunals set up by Act.

manas.q: Which courts are Kenya's superior courts?

children.note: Top court: the Chief Justice (presides), Deputy Chief Justice and five other judges; five judges make a quorum. It hears presidential election disputes first and only, and appeals from the Court of Appeal.

manas.q: Who sits in the Supreme Court and what is its quorum?

children.note: All courts except the Supreme Court itself must follow its decisions. This is precedent written into the Constitution.
It can give advisory opinions on county government matters when asked by the national government, a State organ or a county government.
In September 2017 the Supreme Court cancelled the August presidential result by 4–2, finding the election was not run in line with the Constitution.
Hears appeals from the High Court and from other courts or tribunals named by an Act. It has at least twelve judges, who elect their own President.

manas.q: Where do appeals from the High Court go?

children.note: Unlimited first-instance power in civil and criminal cases. It hears Bill of Rights claims, interprets the Constitution, and supervises subordinate courts and tribunals.

manas.q: What is the High Court's 'supervisory jurisdiction'?

children.topic: What the High Court cannot do
children.note: It has no power over Supreme Court-only matters, or over cases that belong to the Employment and Labour Relations Court or Environment and Land Court. It cannot supervise a superior court.
Parliament must create courts with High Court status for (a) employment and labour disputes and (b) environment and land disputes. These are the ELRC and the ELC.

manas.q: Which two courts have the same status as the High Court?

children.note: A family fight over who owns a shamba in Kiambu goes to the Environment and Land Court (or a magistrate given land powers), not the ordinary High Court.
Where most Kenyans meet the law: traffic cases, small debts, theft charges. Their money limits are set by an Act of Parliament.
Subordinate courts led by a Chief Kadhi, with at least three other Kadhis, all Muslims. Appeals go to the High Court.
Subordinate courts that try members of the Kenya Defence Forces under military law.
Specialist bodies set up by Acts (e.g. on rent, tax, or business premises). They are cheaper and faster than courts but the High Court can supervise them.

children.topic: Judicial authority comes from the people
children.note: Courts hold judicial power on behalf of the people and must do justice to all, avoid delay, and focus on substance over technicalities.

manas.q: Under Article 159, what should courts put ahead of procedural technicalities?

children.note: Judges follow earlier decisions so that like cases are treated alike. Learn which part of a judgment binds and which courts bind which.
Latin for 'stand by what has been decided'. Courts follow earlier rulings on the same legal question, making law predictable and fair.

manas.q: What does stare decisis mean?

children.note: Binding: a lower court must follow it (e.g. a Supreme Court decision). Persuasive: a court may follow it if convinced, e.g. English, Ugandan or Indian decisions in Kenya.

manas.q: What is the difference between binding and persuasive precedent?

children.note: Lower courts must follow higher courts in the same system: a magistrate follows the High Court, the High Court follows the Court of Appeal.
Whether a court must follow its own past decisions. Kenya's Constitution leaves the Supreme Court free to depart from its own earlier rulings.
The legal reason the decision rests on, applied to the key facts. It is the part that binds later courts.

manas.q: What is the ratio decidendi of a case?

children.note: Things a judge says 'by the way' that the decision did not need. They do not bind but can persuade.

manas.q: Are obiter dicta binding?

children.note: To check if a statement is ratio, imagine removing or reversing it. If the outcome would not change, it was obiter.
A court avoids an earlier case by showing the important facts are different, so the old rule does not fit.
A higher court (or the same court where allowed) declares an earlier rule wrong, so it stops being law.
A decision made 'through lack of care', e.g. the court missed a binding statute or case. It may not bind later courts.
Classic cases that teach how precedent works. They come from English law and are persuasive, not binding, in Kenya.
A woman found a decomposed snail in her ginger beer. The House of Lords held a maker owes care to people it can foresee being harmed: the 'neighbour principle', often given as the ratio.

manas.q: What principle came from Donoghue v Stevenson?

children.note: Denning J's remark that a landlord could not reclaim wartime rent was obiter, yet it grew into the modern doctrine of promissory estoppel.
The Lords said, as obiter, that careless advice could make someone liable for pure financial loss, though a disclaimer defeated this claim.
Let the House of Lords depart from its own past decisions when it was right to do so; before then it was strictly bound.
Recognised exceptions, including per incuriam, where the Court of Appeal need not follow its own earlier decision.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
When the words of an Act are unclear, judges use 'rules' of interpretation. Know each rule, one case for it, and its weakness.
Words can be vague, new technology appears, and drafters make mistakes. Is a boda boda a 'motor vehicle'? Is an e-cigarette 'tobacco'? Courts must decide.
Give words their plain, ordinary meaning, even if the result is harsh. Respects Parliament but can produce absurd results.

manas.q: What does the literal rule tell a judge to do?

children.note: The law punished pretending to be 'a person entitled to vote'. The man pretended to be a dead voter; dead people cannot vote, so he was acquitted.
A flick knife in a shop window was not 'offered for sale' in contract law terms, so the shopkeeper's conviction failed. Parliament later fixed the Act.
Start with the plain meaning, but depart from it where it would cause an absurd result (narrow approach) or an outcome against public policy (wide approach).
'In the vicinity of' a military base was read to include being inside it; anything else would be absurd.
A son murdered his mother; the court would not let him (or his heirs) inherit from her, as that would reward the crime.
Ask what problem (mischief) the Act was made to cure, then read it to stop that problem. Comes from Heydon's Case (1584) and its four questions.

manas.q: What four questions does Heydon's Case ask?

children.note: Women soliciting from balconies and windows were held to be soliciting 'in the street', because the Act aimed to stop street harassment.
Read the words in light of the law's whole purpose, using wider material if needed. The leading modern approach in most common-law courts.
The House of Lords allowed courts to look at statements in Parliament when an Act is ambiguous and strict conditions are met.
It must be read to promote its purposes, values and principles, the rule of law and the Bill of Rights, and good governance: a purposive approach written into the text.

manas.q: How must the Constitution of Kenya be interpreted?

children.note: The Constitution is read as speaking in the present, so powers pass to whoever holds an office now and to successor bodies.
Internal: the long title, definitions section, headings. External: dictionaries, reports, Hansard. In Kenya, also the Interpretation and General Provisions Act.

children.topic: 6. How to read, reason and answer
children.note: Practical method: pull the rule out of a case, break down a statute, and write a clear answer.
Case name, citation, court, judges, date, headnote (an editor's summary), then the judgment(s). The headnote is not law; read the judgment itself.
Note the Facts, the Issue (question for the court), the Rule applied, the Application (reasoning) and the Conclusion. Keep a one-page brief for each case.

children.topic: Find the ratio, not the story
children.note: Ask: what were the key facts, and what rule did the court need to decide them? Separate that from side comments and dissents.
Check the long title and purpose, the definitions section, the section you need, and its subsections and exceptions. Then check if it is in force and amended.
'Shall' usually means must; 'may' usually means can choose. 'And' joins conditions; 'or' gives options. Small words change outcomes.
Issue → Rule → Application → Conclusion. Name the issue, state the rule with authority, apply it to the facts, then reach a clear conclusion.

manas.q: What does IRAC stand for?

children.note: A new county by-law bans 'hooting in town'. Wanjiru's matatu driver hoots to warn a child on the road and is charged. Did he break the by-law?
Issue: does 'hooting' cover a warning hoot? Rules: the literal rule (any hoot), golden rule (avoid absurdity), mischief/purposive (the by-law targets noise, not safety).
A literal reading punishes a safety act, an absurd result. The purpose was noise control, so a court would likely read in a safety exception. Conclusion: probably not guilty.

children.topic: Exam trap: mixing ratio and obiter
children.note: Do not quote a judge's passing remark as binding law. Say which part is ratio, and call obiter 'persuasive'.

children.topic: Exam trap: English cases as binding
children.note: English cases are persuasive in Kenya, not binding. Always check for a Kenyan authority and the Constitution first.
Every Kenyan law question starts at the top of the ladder. Check whether the Constitution answers or limits the point.
Land and labour disputes go to the ELC and ELRC, not the High Court. Kadhis' courts are subordinate courts, not superior ones.
Naming all four interpretation rules earns little. Apply the most fitting one to the facts and explain why.
Who lawyers are in Kenya and how a law graduate becomes an advocate.
Lawyers admitted to practise before Kenyan courts. Kenya has one fused profession: an advocate can both advise clients and argue in court.
The Act that governs who may practise as an advocate, admission to the Roll, practising certificates and discipline.
The professional body for advocates, set up under the Law Society of Kenya Act. Membership is needed to practise; it runs continuing professional development and speaks on justice issues.

manas.q: What is the Law Society of Kenya?

children.note: Regulates legal education: accredits and licenses law schools, sets core courses, and has run the Bar examination since the 2014 amendments.

manas.q: Which body sets the Bar examination in Kenya?

children.note: Kenya's bar school in Nairobi. Graduates take the Advocates Training Programme: about 12 months of classes plus 6 months of pupillage.
LLB degree → Advocates Training Programme at KSL with pupillage → pass CLE Bar exams → admission to the Roll by the Chief Justice → LSK practising certificate. Reviewer: confirm steps.
Practical training under an experienced advocate, a little like an internship. Pupils draft, research and attend court.
Judges and magistrates, state counsel, prosecutors (ODPP), in-house counsel, legal researchers, and paralegals who support lawyers.
